newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir leader would shed blood for India.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir leader would shed blood for India.

text.p: Farooq Abdullah, who tearfully took office as chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state on Wednesday, has devoted his life to defending India's claim over the rebellious region.
"The last drop of my blood will go to defend India," Abdullah said in an emotional speech taking oath. "Kashmir has been, is, and always will be, part of India."
Abdullah, 59, has returned from nearly seven years in the political wilderness to walk a tightrope between separatists and federal politicians in New Delhi.

His National Conference party emphatically won last month's state elections. Abdullah escaped two grenade attacks during the campaign in which 21 activists, most of them from his party, were killed in clashes with separatists.
But there are many in Kashmir who say the 59-year-old leader failed the test during his previous tenures as chief minister.

"He cannot solve anything," said lawyer and separatist leader Pir Hafizullah Makhdoomi, who argued that Farooq's party had alienated many former supporters. "He has come into the political process only to save his own party."

The British-trained doctor with a taste for the high life was last elected chief minister in 1987 in a controversial poll alliance with India's Congress party, which many Kashmiris say sowed the seeds of a rebellion in 1990.
Abdullah was accused by rivals of rigging the elections, which critics say forced rivals to support separatism.
New Delhi dismissed Abdullah's government in 1990, saying he was soft on rebels, and deployed tens of thousands of soldiers and paramilitary troops.
Since then, police and hospital sources estimate 20,000 people have died in the violence.
Despite widespread disenchantment with his rule, Abdullah remains a towering leader in the state, thanks mainly to his father, Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah.

For most Kashmiris, Farooq Abdullah still wears the mantle and carries the credibility of his father, the "Lion of Kashmir", who dominated regional politics for half a century, much of it from jail, before dying in 1982.
Farooq, who told Reuters he felt like "a tiger out of the woods" on returning to power, has been chief minister of Kashmir three times in the past.
"The biggest challenge for me is to bring peace to Kashmir and wipe out the gun," Farooq said recently. "To enable people to realise their dreams and generate employment for the youth."
The National Conference stayed out of general elections in May, saying the federal government, then led by Congress, was not seriously committed to granting Kashmir greater autonomy.
But Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition pledged "maxiumum autonomy" after assuming power in June.
Abdullah has said he wants the restoration of powers which before 1952 lay in the state's hands but which have since been seized by the federal government.
The Indian constitution gives the state nominal charge of all areas but communications, defence and foreign relations.
The constitution also gave the state the right to select its own Sadar-e-Riyasat, or president, who could not be dismissed by New Delhi without the state government's consent.
Farooq, whose wife is British, has a penchant for night life and spent much of the past six years in London, stirring animosity among some Kashmiris.

But he has a tough streak. Recently he said separatists "must be made to suffer", and he pledged to crack down on armed militants. But he persists in efforts to open talks with unarmed separatists, who rejected his initial overture.
